transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2026-08-30 15:00 UTC
Duration: 90 minutes
Attendees: Ethan Park (Redwood AE), Sanjay Rao (Redwood SE), Maya Li (Redwood SE), Priya Menon (Halo ML Infra), Jamal Ortiz (Halo CTO), Ling Zhao (Halo NLP Eng), Oscar Varela (Halo Security)

Summary (auto): technical deep dive on long-context runtime strategies for 128k+ prompts, chunking and eviction policies for KV cache, quantization tradeoffs, and on-prem/VPC considerations. Action items captured.

Topics: runtime batching, KV cache sharding, eviction, hierarchical chunking, sliding-sparse attention, quantization profiles (int8/Q4), VPC/on-prem install constraints, SOC2/KMS

--- Transcript ---
[00:00:07] Ethan Park: all right everyone, thanks for hopping on. We'll kick off — today's goal is to walk through how Redwood handles extremely long contexts (128k and up) end-to-end and get specific on eviction and chunking strategy for Halo's streaming transcripts.
[00:00:22] Priya Menon: thanks, Ethan. we want to understand the cost/latency trade-offs for a streaming robot telemetry use case where a single session can hit ~1M tokens over 24 hours, but the hot working set is more like 100k to 250k.
[00:00:34] Sanjay Rao: great, that's exactly the pattern we optimized for in the recent beta — two mental models: the mounted context pipeline which treats the full transcript as an append-only store, and the working-set cache (KV) that keeps most-recent and most-relevant spans in fast memory.
[00:00:44] Jamal Ortiz: can you clarify mounted context pipeline — is that basically a filesystem-backed chain of chunks?
[00:00:49] Sanjay Rao: yes, more or less. we chunk incoming tokens into sized shards (e.g., 8k or 16k) with metadata pointers. On read we'll stitch chunks with a lightweight index to avoid re-concatenation cost. For very long histories we keep cold chunks on SSD/NVMe and the hot KV entries in GPU DRAM.
[00:01:06] Ling Zhao: and how do you decide chunk size? we saw guidance ranging 2k–32k.
[00:01:12] Maya Li: a lot depends on model receptive field and attention pattern. smaller chunks reduce wasted context when you have narrow windows, but increase lookup overhead. for our 128k targets we like 8k–16k chunking with hierarchical retrieval — i.e., gather chunk summaries, then expand top-K chunk bodies into KV lookups.
[00:01:28] Priya Menon: okay but the expensive part is the KV cache growth — if we keep every token in KV for all sessions we'll need hundreds of GB of GPU RAM. what's Redwood's eviction policy?
[00:01:37] Sanjay Rao: we run a segmented-LFU by default for streaming workloads — frequency-weighted but biased to recency. that avoids thrashing when old tokens are occasionally referenced. there's also a time-decay variant and a TTL per-session policy. for some workloads TTL + size cap is simplest.
[00:01:49] Jamal Ortiz: segmented-LFU sounds promising. do you support pinning keys for explicit retention? for example, flags to pin last N steps of a control loop?
[00:01:56] Sanjay Rao: yes — pinning is supported at the API level. you can mark ranges as sticky which move them to a hot tier and exempt them from eviction except via admin ops.
[00:02:06] Oscar Varela: security question — when KV is sharded across GPUs, how do logs look and what about KMS integration for on-prem?
[00:02:12] Maya Li: we stream audit logs to the control plane (for hosted) or to your syslog/ELK in private installs. KMS is pluggable — HSM/KMS calls happen in the control-plane handshake and never at per-token rate. on-prem bundle includes connectors for Vault and cloud KMS.
[00:02:24] Priya Menon: what about performance numbers — latencies for full context retrieval vs hot-KV hits?
[00:02:30] Sanjay Rao: hot KV hit for 128k-ish sessions is generally sub-50ms for the KV lookup and concat step on A100 class GPUs; end-to-end token generation latency depends on batching and kernel selection — for small single-user streaming with minimal batching we see ~120–250ms per token on Q4 quantized paths; with batching across 8–16 concurrent streams you can push amortized per-token to ~60–90ms.
[00:02:47] Jamal Ortiz: those sound optimistic — are those numbers for one-step generation or for full next-token decode in-chat?
[00:02:52] Sanjay Rao: next token decode, i.e., the full LM forward pass with KV attend. the split is roughly KV lookup (0.03–0.05s) + kernel attention + softmax. quantization impacts kernel speed dramatically — Q4 kernels are about 1.6x slower than int8 fast paths but have better quality in some models.
[00:03:07] Ling Zhao: can Redwood run mixed-precision per-layer so we keep attention layers int8 and feedforward q4?
[00:03:13] Sanjay Rao: yes, we support hybrid quantization profiles per model. the optimizer chooses layerwise quant scheme and can be overridden. the console exposes a profile diff so you can see expected latency and potential perplexity delta.
[00:03:24] Priya Menon: for our workload, we have lots of long but sparse references — controllers occasionally reference a log entry from hours earlier. how does retrieval work without scanning the whole context?
[00:03:32] Maya Li: two strategies: first, hierarchical chunking and light-weight LLM reranker — we index chunk embeddings (coarse) and run a cheap reranker to pick top candidate chunks, then expand. second, sparse attention primitives — sliding windows + global tokens so the model can focus on local context and a few global anchors.
[00:03:47] Jamal Ortiz: does the runtime support sparse attention natively or is it model-level?
[00:03:51] Sanjay Rao: runtime supports optimized sparse ops (block-sparse and sliding-window) for supported architectures. we also do kernel selection so if the model is configured for sparse attention the runtime picks the sparse kernel; if not, it falls back to dense.
[00:04:02] Priya Menon: the eviction behavior in practice — do you have dashboards that show cache hit-rate by session?
[00:04:06] Maya Li: yes, per-session KV hit-rates, token-level cost, and heatmaps. we surfaced an eviction simulator in the console recently — you can feed in a representative trace and simulate LRU/LFU/TTL and see hit-rate vs GPU RAM curve.
[00:04:18] Ling Zhao: I like that — can we run our sample trace through the simulator?
[00:04:21] Ethan Park: absolutely, that's one of the next steps — Priya, if you can share a trace we'll run it and return a recommended config.
[00:04:28] Priya Menon: yes. we'll anonymize. also two more things: quantization impact on rollbacks and model fidelity — we saw hallucination rates increase with heavier quant.
[00:04:36] Sanjay Rao: totally expected — quantization profile tuning plus eval prompt-sets are how we control that. Redwood Optimize can run regression tests on your prompt suite and flag quality deltas when a quant profile or model change would impact outputs.
[00:04:47] Jamal Ortiz: Ops question — for on-prem, what's the network topology? do we need a persistent control-plane connection?
[00:04:52] Maya Li: private deployments can run in two flavors: disconnected on-prem bundle (air-gapped with outbound-only licensing handshake) or VPC-connected where the control plane is in Redwood but telemetry and payloads stay in your VPC. the control-plane handshake is periodic and uses mTLS; you can opt for a full on-prem control plane for enterprise.
[00:05:05] Oscar Varela: that helps. latency fingerprinting — when you shard KV across GPUs, how do you avoid cross-GPU communication for typical lookups?
[00:05:12] Sanjay Rao: we prefer horizontal partitioning by session and localize hot keys within a GPU. for lookups that span partitions we do asynchronous prefetch and priority routing. the typical path is single-GPU read; cross-GPU happens but we try to amortize via batching and overlap comms with compute.
[00:05:26] Priya Menon: what about eviction thresholds — do you set them per-GPU or globally?
[00:05:30] Sanjay Rao: mostly per-GPU with a global balancing controller that migrates hot keys if a GPU becomes a hotspot. migration is cheap because keys are chunk pointers; we move pointer ownership and optionally pre-warm key values.
[00:05:42] Ling Zhao: can we force a policy that retains last 200k tokens for safety-critical sessions?
[00:05:46] Maya Li: yes, via session-level retention config. caveat: retaining 200k tokens per session on GPU means you need large-GPU pools or dedicated capacity; we can model the cost and show trade-offs.
[00:05:56] Jamal Ortiz: curious about storage tiering — is cold chunking standard SSD, or do you recommend NVMe or S3?
[00:06:00] Sanjay Rao: cold chunks can live on S3 for very large archives, but for reasonable retrieval latency we recommend NVMe-local SSDs. our private bundle supports NVMe-backed nodes and an LRU local store before falling back to S3.
[00:06:11] Priya Menon: for the 1M token transcripts we discussed, what's the recommended indexing cadence? do you index every chunk at ingest or on first read?
[00:06:17] Sanjay Rao: hybrid approach — we compute lightweight embeddings at ingest for every chunk (cheap) and keep a Bloom-filter-like summary for quick exclusion. heavy reranking vectors are computed lazily on first read for rarely-accessed chunks.
[00:06:28] Ling Zhao: how do you handle sequential consistency for append-only streams across restarts?
[00:06:32] Maya Li: we use monotonic commit logs with an append-only ledger per session. the runtime can replay to recreate KV entries; there's a checkpointing cadence to bound replay time.
[00:06:41] Priya Menon: let's talk quantization specifics — you mentioned Q4 earlier. can you say more about Q4 variants and accuracy hit?
[00:06:47] Sanjay Rao: Q4 formats (Q4_0, Q4_K_M variants) differ by scale and per-channel vs per-tensor. we ship a tuning profile that picks the least-impactful scheme per layer. generally, Q4 gives better memory density than int8 for some transformer blocks but runtime cost is higher due to bit unpacking; net effect depends on model architecture.
[00:07:01] Jamal Ortiz: do you support online re-quant (re-quantizing a model in-place)?
[00:07:05] Sanjay Rao: we support in-place re-quant with a roll-forward canary — we spin up a canary model with new quant and shadow traffic and run A/B checks on your eval set.
[00:07:13] Priya Menon: the canary process is important for us — we need automated rollback on quality regression.
[00:07:17] Maya Li: rollback is automated if the eval metrics cross your threshold; we keep previous version pinned for quick fallback.
[00:07:23] Oscar Varela: how do we ensure telemetry doesn't leak PII into logs when running on-prem?
[00:07:28] Maya Li: for private installs logs can be configured to mask or filter fields; audit logs can be redacted. plus we support token-level encryption in flight and at rest with your KMS.
[00:07:37] Ling Zhao: I'd like a walkthrough of the eviction simulator interface — metrics and knobs
[00:07:41] Ethan Park: Sanjay, do you want to demo the simulator for 10 minutes?
[00:07:44] Sanjay Rao: sure — sharing screen. (brief screen share sounds)
[00:07:52] [00:07:52] Sanjay Rao: okay, here's the simulator — ingest a trace, pick chunk size, pick policy (LRU/LFU/time-decay), set GPU RAM target, and run. you get time-series hit-rate, percent of hits coming from hot tier, and expected cost per 1M tokens.
[00:08:08] Priya Menon: what's the cost model anchored to? raw token cost or GPU-hour?
[00:08:12] Sanjay Rao: GPU-hour + token compute + storage egress if any. for dedicated/private we model GPU instance types and local NVMe.
[00:08:21] Ling Zhao: can the simulator emit a recommended config?
[00:08:24] Sanjay Rao: yes, it suggests chunk size, retention windows, and a baseline quant profile. it's heuristic but useful.
[00:08:30] Priya Menon: let's run our anonymized 72-hour trace.
[00:08:33] Ethan Park: perfect. we'll collect the trace offline — next steps.
[00:08:38] [00:08:38] Jamal Ortiz: shifting gears — what about throughput under heavy concurrent decode? we need sustained 200 concurrent sessions each with moderate request rates.
[00:08:47] Sanjay Rao: two levers: batching and autoscaling. continuous batching aggregates small requests across sessions into larger kernels; it increases throughput but can increase tail latency. autoscaling for Dedicated can add GPU nodes within seconds using burst capacity. for VPC/on-prem autoscaling requires orchestrator (we ship Helm charts for k8s with the autoscaler).
[00:09:05] Priya Menon: is there a best practice for setting batch windows?
[00:09:08] Maya Li: start with an adaptive window: target batch size of 4–8 for interactive workloads, increase to 16–32 for throughput-oriented tasks. Redwood's runtime includes an adaptive algorithm that widens the window when queue time is low and tightens it when you see latency SLO breaches.
[00:09:22] Ling Zhao: show us how fallback routing works if a model variant is out of capacity.
[00:09:26] Sanjay Rao: policy-based routing — you can set rules: fall back by latency tolerance (if SLO tight, route to faster smaller model), or by cost. routing can also prefer private capacity first then hosted bursting.
[00:09:36] Priya Menon: for long sessions do you ever compress chunks via summary tokens to reduce KV size?
[00:09:41] Maya Li: yes, we support lossy compression strategies and learned summarizers. you can keep a denser summary for very old segments and only decompress if the reranker signals relevance.
[00:09:52] Jamal Ortiz: curious about kernel scheduling — do you schedule attention and KV fetches overlapping to hide comms?
[00:09:56] Sanjay Rao: yes. we pipeline KV fetch, prefetch keys for predicted next chunks, and schedule compute to overlap network transfers. it reduces visible latencies especially for cross-node fetches.
[00:10:06] Ling Zhao: are there any gotchas for model authors when designing for mounted contexts?
[00:10:10] Sanjay Rao: model authors should be careful about positional encodings beyond their native pos limit. we use a relative-positioning scheme for long contexts but prompt engineering to include anchors and global tokens is helpful. also avoid attention patterns that require dense all-to-all for whole history.
[00:10:23] Priya Menon: one more compliance quick question — for VPC we need audit trails that are immutable for 7 years. supported?
[00:10:30] Maya Li: we can configure append-only audit logs pushed to your archival storage; retention is configurable and we can support immutability via object-lock on S3 or WORM store on-prem.
[00:10:40] Ethan Park: good. time check — we've covered a lot. any last clarifying questions?
[00:10:45] Priya Menon: can you summarize recommended starting config for Halo?
[00:10:48] Ethan Park: sure — high level: 8k chunks, segmented-LFU with last-200k pin option for critical sessions, NVMe local cold tier + S3 archive, hybrid quant profile with attention layers prioritized for higher precision, adaptive batching targeting 8 concurrent aggregations, and run the eviction simulator on your anonymized trace.
[00:11:04] Jamal Ortiz: that sounds actionable. we'll sign up for the PoC if the numbers look right.
[00:11:08] Ling Zhao: can you also include recommendations for model parallelism/placement?
[00:11:11] Sanjay Rao: yes — we'll include node type recommendations (A100-80GB vs H100) and whether to use tensor-parallel or expert-sharded placement for the specific model size.
[00:11:20] [01:27:10] Ethan Park: (closing) thanks everyone — recap in email, and we'll attach the simulator output and the benchmark harness.
[01:27:22] Priya Menon: thanks — appreciate the depth.
[01:27:28] Jamal Ortiz: thanks.
[01:27:35] Ling Zhao: bye.
[01:27:40] Oscar Varela: bye.
